subtopic: 11.02 Code Of Ethics And Standards Of Professional Conduct
question_en: A client names a Member in a written complaint involving potential misconduct and files the complaint with the Member's firm. At a minimum, CFA Institute's Code and Standards require that the Member:
option_a: self-disclose the incident on the annual Professional Conduct Statement.
option_b: immediately disclose the incident to CFA Institute's Professional Conduct Program staff.
option_c: self-disclose the incident on the annual Professional Conduct Statement only if the firm finds
explanation_en:
Professional conduct
All Members and Candidates must file an annual Professional Conduct Statement
Any matter that questions professional conduct must be disclosed
Written complaints sent directly to CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program staff can result in an investigation
CFA Institute staff may also investigate if they become aware of questionable conduct
The CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program provides a framework for handling inquiries about Members' and Candidates' professional
conduct. The Professional Conduct Program staff can initiate an inquiry based on either an external complaint or an internal investigation. The
staff works with the Disciplinary Review Committee to enforce the Code and Standards.
Members and Candidates are required to submit a completed Professional Conduct Statement annually. This statement is a pledge to adhere to
the Code and Standards and the Professional Conduct Program. It also provides an opportunity to self-disclose questionable behavior.
When a Member or Candidate receives a written complaint that questions his or her professional conduct, the complaint must be disclosed to
Professional Conduct Program staff. CFA Institute encourages disclosure at the time of the event, but at a minimum the matter must be disclosed
when filing the annual Professional Conduct Statement (Choice B).
(Choice C) Regardless of the outcome of any internal (ie, firm) investigation, the Member or Candidate must self-disclose the incident on the
annual Professional Conduct Statement or directly to Professional Conduct Program staff.

subtopic: 11.02 Code Of Ethics And Standards Of Professional Conduct
question_en: Which of the following statements best describes the obligation of Members and Candidates with respect to the Standards of Professional Conduct? When in an advisory relationship with a client, they must determine investment suitability based on only:
option_a: the merits of that specific investment.
option_b: earning the highest returns with the lowest fees.
option_c: the client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints.
explanation_en:
"When Members and Candidates are in an advisory relationship with a client, they must:
a. Make a reasonable inquiry into a client's or prospective client's investment experience, risk and return objectives, and financial
constraints prior to making any investment recommendation or taking investment action and must reassess and update this
information regularly.
b. Determine that an investment is suitable to the client's financial situation and consistent with the client's written objectives,
mandates, and constraints before making an investment recommendation or taking investment action.
c. Judge the suitability of investments in the context of the client's total portfolio."
CFA Members (including CFA charterholders) and Candidates are obligated to abide by and advocate for the Code of Ethics (ie, the Code) and the
Standards of Professional Conduct (ie, the Standards), which provide guidance for appropriate ethical behavior. The Code includes general
principles to which Members and Candidates must adhere. In contrast, the Standards address the principles' more specific applications, which
must be followed.
Standard III(C) Suitability addresses the Members' and Candidates' responsibilities to assess the suitability of investments for each client. A
Member or Candidate does this by researching each client's specific investment goals, constraints, and risk tolerance, which are compared to the
characteristics of each proposed investment. Specifically, a Member or Candidate must determine suitability based on a client's written
objectives, mandates, and constraints before taking investment action.
(Choice A) Investment suitability is based not only on the merits of a specific investment but also how that investment fits within a client's total
portfolio.
(Choice B) Low-fee investments are preferred if they are suitable and appropriate. However, the highest expected return may entail greater risk
(ie, returns cannot be ensured) than a client is willing or able to bear and so may not be suitable for that client.

subtopic: 11.02 Code Of Ethics And Standards Of Professional Conduct
question_en: According to The Code of Ethics, members and candidates are most likely required to:
option_a: try to improve the competence of other investment professionals.
option_b: place clients' interests above the integrity of the investment profession.
option_c: promote the integrity of the global markets regardless of its effect on society.
explanation_en:
The Code of Ethics (ie, the Code) identifies six components of aspirational behavior that prescribe how members and candidates must act. One
component of the Code is to "strive to maintain and improve the competence of other investment professionals." In addition to maintaining
and improving their own professional expertise, members and candidates must help other investment professionals do the same.
(Choice B) The Code requires that members and candidates place the integrity of the profession and the interests of clients before the
members' or candidates' interests. It is a misinterpretation of the Code to place client interests ahead of the integrity of the profession.
(Choice C) The Code requires members and candidates to "promote the integrity and viability of the global capital markets for the ultimate
benefit of society."

question_en: Himari Sato just got home from taking Level I of the CFA exam. She goes onto a popular online forum and writes, "Just got back from Level I. Definitely a hard exam, much harder than I expected based on my studying, but I think I passed! However, I still disagree with CFA Institute's policy of providing ranges for the weights of each subject on the exam. Just tell us what to expect! I studied way too hard for derivatives, but the number of questions was at the bottom of the range. I wasted so much time on this." Sato violated the Standards by:
option_a: disagreeing with CFA Institute's exam policies.
option_b: expressing an opinion on the difficulty of the exam.
option_c: providing information about topics tested on the exam.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must understand and comply with all applicable laws, rules, and regulations (including the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct) of any government, regulatory organization, licensing agency, or professional association governing their professional activities. In the event of conflict, Members and Candidates must comply with the more strict law, rule, or regulation…." Investment professionals often work with clients located in different countries with laws and regulations that might conflict with local laws. Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law mandates that Members and Candidates resolve conflicts that arise when laws of different countries require different actions in a given situation. In the CFA Code and Standards, the basic rule for "choice-of-law" issues is that the Member (or Candidate) must always adhere to the strictest given law. However, if the Code and Standards impose stricter requirements than the law of the Member's home country or the country where the Member is doing business, the member must follow the Code and Standards. In this scenario, Countries X and Y both require her to take some action, so she would not be acting appropriately by doing nothing even though her own country's laws are silent on the issue (Choices A and C).

question_en: Bernard Logan, CFA, manages a small-cap growth exchange-traded fund (ETF) for Firefly Capital. Logan's boss is concerned that the ETF's trading volume is low compared to that of peers. He directs Logan to determine which of the firm's largest investors the ETF would be suitable for, and then ask those investors to agree to purchase fixed amounts of the ETF at regular intervals over the next month. Investors that agree to do so will pay reduced commissions. The boss expects that the larger number of trades will support market liquidity for the ETF and create greater interest among potential investors, which will benefit the existing clients who invest in the ETF. The boss asks that Logan not disclose this arrangement to the general investing public. To comply with Standard II(B) Market Manipulation, Logan's best course of action is to:
option_a: suggest Firefly disclose the agreements before proceeding.
option_b: proceed with his boss's request without disclosing the agreements.
option_c: tell his boss that such agreements violate the Standards even if they are disclosed.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must understand and comply with all applicable laws, rules, and regulations (including the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct) of any government, regulatory organization, licensing agency, or professional association governing their professional activities. In the event of conflict, Members and Candidates must comply with the more strict law, rule, or regulation...." Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law prescribes how Members and Candidates resolve conflicts when the applicable laws of a jurisdiction conflict with behaviors required by the CFA Institute Code and Standards. The general rule is that Members and Candidates must adhere to the stricter of: the laws and regulations in their home country and the Code and Standards. In this scenario, the laws of Hella Flosadottir's country (Country A) are less strict than both the Code and Standards and the laws of Country B. Country B's laws are stricter than the Code and Standards, so Flosadottir's most appropriate action is to contact the Country B police. (Choices B and C) Country A's laws would require Flosadottir to notify the client; the Code and Standards require her to seek guidance from her firm's compliance officer. However, since both options are less strict than the laws of Country B, Country B's laws apply.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
question_en: Haley Jarwin, CFA, lives in Country Z. She recently joined a new investment bank located in Country X. Country X's securities require that the laws of a client's home country shall govern if the client is not located in Country X. Jarwin is assigned to work on a large IPO for a client that is located in Country Y, whose securities laws are less strict than those of Country X. Jarwin believes some of the client's confidential financial information is fraudulent and may be evidence of criminal activity. Country X's laws require that she report her suspicions to securities regulators, but Country Y's laws prohibit reporting unless the client is first requested to remedy the fraud and refuses to act. Country Z has no laws that apply to this situation. Under Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law, Jarwin's least appropriate course of action is to:
option_a: report the fraud to the Country X regulators.
option_b: do nothing since Country Z has no laws that apply.
option_c: request that the client amend the financial information so that it is not fraudulent.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment. Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their client's interests before their employer's or their own interests." Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care requires Members and Candidates to be loyal to their clients and to use prudence and care when making investment decisions on a client's behalf. This first step is properly identifying the client. For Members and Candidates in an advisory role, the client is the service's investors or beneficiaries. In cases where the Member or Candidate is a fund manager, the client is not an investor or beneficiary but the investment fund and its mandate. In this scenario, Latha Mani manages an index fund with a specific mandate. Although the fund has investors, those investors may enter and exit the fund of their own accord. Mani is not their advisor and therefore does not owe them her loyalty (Choice A). Mani must be loyal to managing the fund to its mandate since investors have made investment decisions based on the expectation of using Mani's fund to gain exposure to small cap growth stocks. Deviating from that mandate would breach clients' trust. (Choice C) Although Mani owes loyalty to her employer and its shareholders, clients or fund investors take precedence before employers. Therefore, Mani's primary duty of loyalty is owed to managing the fund to its mandate.

question_en: Latha Mani, CFA, manages an index fund with a small-cap growth mandate. The fund is owned by Alpha Investments and has thousands of investors. Mani's primary duty of loyalty is to:
option_a: the investors in the fund.
option_b: operate the fund to its mandate.
option_c: Alpha Investments' shareholders.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved." Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements notes that third-party, additional compensation is allowed. However, if the arrangement could be reasonably seen as creating a conflict with the employer, the Member or Candidate must obtain written permission from all parties involved. In this case, continuing her advising activities could reasonably be seen as presenting a conflict with Kim's agreed-upon, diminished role at the firm. Kim would be required to obtain written permission from both the client and her employer. (Choice A) Kim's duty of loyalty does not require her to refuse the offer; she may accept it if she first obtains written permission from all parties. (Choice B) Merely informing her employer is not quite enough; Kim must get the employer's written permission as an involved party before she can accept the offer.

question_en: Jacqueline Dumont, CFA, is an adviser to high-net-worth clients. For over 20 years, she advised Marc and Denise Paraguet, who divorced three years ago. As a condition of the divorce, all of their joint accounts were closed, and their assets were divided between them. After the divorce was settled at the end of 20X1, Denise Paraguet remained Dumont's client for one year, then ended their advisory relationship and moved her investments to another firm. Marc Paraguet, who remains a client of Dumont's, recently asked Dumont for information about Denise's investment activities during 20X2, when she was still Dumont's client. To comply with Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality, which of the following is Dumont's best course of action?
option_a: Share the information since Marc is her client.
option_b: Do not share the information since Denise was her client.
option_c: Share the information since Denise is no longer her client.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved." Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements requires Members and Candidates to obtain written permission when third-party, additional compensation agreements could be reasonably seen as creating a conflict with their employers. Permission must be received from all parties before the agreement can be accepted. The Standard applies to both monetary and nonmonetary (eg, gifts, benefits) compensation. In this scenario, accepting Jain's offer to pay for quarterly dinners to discuss portfolio allocation could be perceived as a conflict of interest since Patel's actions can be perceived as giving Jain preferential treatment. His advice could be viewed as favoring Jain over his own clients and may run counter to advice given by Eclipse's other advisers. To comply with the Standard, Patel would be required to obtain written permission from both Jain and Eclipse before accepting the offer so Eclipse can monitor his actions. (Choice A) Patel is not required to reject the offer so long as he obtains written permission from all parties involved so his employer can monitor for conflicts. (Choice B) Informing Eclipse after accepting the offer is a violation of the Standard. Patel must receive permission before agreeing so Eclipse can decide if the agreement presents a conflict.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
question_en: Grace Kim, CFA, has been an adviser to clients at Keundon Investments for 10 years. Kim negotiates with Keundon to cut back her hours to 20 per week (from 50) to allow her to manage her father's care. Kim agrees to give up her advising role and work in the firm's back office. She will be paid 25% of her usual salary, but she hopes to eventually return to full-time advising. Kim informs clients of her new role and that they will have a new adviser at the firm. The next day, one of her clients offers to pay her to confidentially review any recommendations he receives from another adviser, as he trusts her judgment. To comply with Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements, which of the following actions is most likely required of Kim?
option_a: Refuse the client's offer
option_b: Accept the offer and inform her employer in writing
option_c: Obtain written permission from her employer before accepting the offer
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants." Standard II(B) Market Manipulation prohibits activities by Members or Candidates that deceive market participants by distorting securities prices or volumes. Manipulation can occur through: information-based activities (eg, issuing false or misleading information) and/or transaction-based activities (eg, exaggerated trading between two accounts). The Standard does not prevent the use of legitimate trading strategies, even if they cause price movements or are designed to purposefully limit the impact on the market. The key element in determining whether the Standard is violated is intent: if the strategy is intended to deceive investors, it violates the Standard. In this scenario, if Zhao Fen traded Formula Industries stock between her personal accounts, it would give market participants a false impression of higher trading volume since the trading is not done between unique market participants. Deceiving participants through transaction-based manipulation violates the Standard. (Choice A) Using an intermediary (eg, block house) to sell the position outside the market or break the order into smaller batches is a legitimate trading strategy. This practice aims to reduce a sale's impact on the market, but the resulting trades are done with other market participants and therefore do not violate the Standard. (Choice B) While selling all the holdings in one position might drive down the price, Zhao may do so without intending to manipulate market participants; therefore, it is not the action most likely to violate the Standard. The Standards do not require Members or Candidates to disadvantage themselves to uphold market integrity, so this strategy can be used if cash is needed quickly.

option_a: Patel must reject the offer

option_c: Patel can accept the offer only after disclosing it in writing to Eclipse and receiving approval
explanation_en:

interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved."
Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements requires Members and Candidates to obtain written permission when third-party,
additional compensation agreements could be reasonably seen as creating a conflict with their employers. Permission must be received from
all parties before the agreement can be accepted. The Standard applies to both monetary and nonmonetary (eg, gifts, benefits) compensation.

question_en: Champion Partners is an asset management firm that employs both Charterholders and non-Charterholders as portfolio managers. Lorraine Dubois, CFA, is a portfolio manager for Champion who wishes to use third-party research reports in her investment process. Champion's portfolio managers are allowed to use third-party research only from firms whose research is vetted by the firm's senior managers. Dubois receives a report from Dominion Financial, one of the third-party research firms approved by Champion's senior managers. To comply with the Standards, most likely Dubois:
option_a: cannot use any third-party research in her process.
option_b: can use the research report without further due diligence.
option_c: must conduct her own due diligence on the third-party research.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must understand and comply with all applicable laws, rules, and regulations (including the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct) of any government, regulatory organization, licensing agency, or professional association governing their professional activities. In the event of conflict, Members and Candidates must comply with the more strict law, rule, or regulation. Members and Candidates must not knowingly participate or assist in and must dissociate from any violation of such laws, rules, or regulations." To abide by Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law, Members and Candidates who create financial products that will be sold in more than one country must comply with each country's laws and regulations. When the laws conflict, Members and Candidates must comply with the stricter law. However, if the Code and Standards are stricter than the country's laws, then Members and Candidates must adhere to the Code and Standards. In this scenario, Karl Mahler must compare the laws in the country where the product originated with the laws in the additional country where it will be sold and compare both with the Code and Standards. The laws in Country A, the country of origin, are stricter than the Code and Standards, so when Mahler sells the mutual fund in Country A, he must adhere to the laws of Country A. The laws in Country B, the additional country of sale, also are more strict than the Code and Standards, so Country B's laws take precedence (Choice C). However, the laws in Country B are less strict than those in Country A, so Mahler must adhere to Country A's laws when he sells the mutual fund in Country B. Country A's laws are the most strict of the three possibilities (Choice B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
question_en: Naomi Jorgensen, CFA, a broker at Belton Financial, Inc., currently has a sell rating on Alpha Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (API) due to its lackluster pipeline of therapeutics. Derek DiGravio, CFA, an investment banker at Belton, is helping API with its next round of funding and believes that if API receives an additional cash infusion, it will be very successful. DiGravio suggests to Jorgensen that she should reconsider her rating. To comply with Standard I(B) Independence and Objectively, Jorgenson's best course of action is to:
option_a: request reassignment of security coverage.
option_b: rate API only as a hold until corroborating public information is available.
option_c: update clients with publicly available information but abstain from giving API a rating.
explanation_en: "In matters related to their employment, Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their employer and not deprive their employer of the advantage of their skills and abilities, divulge confidential information, or otherwise cause harm to their employer." Standard IV Duties to Employers addresses the Member or Candidate's responsibilities as an employee. Standard IV(A) Loyalty notes that Members and Candidates must try to protect the interests of their employer and avoid actions that may harm those interests. Before leaving an employer, a Member or Candidate must follow its policies and procedures for notifying clients and must not make any attempt to solicit clients for another firm. After leaving an employer, the Member or Candidate can solicit former clients as long as the contact information used is not the property of the former employer. In this case, Ostrovsky did not mention either his departure from BII or his future plans to his BII clients before leaving BII, and he did not use BII's proprietary data to contact them, so he has not violated the Standard (Choices B and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
question_en: Hans Mohr, CFA, manages the Matrix European Stock Index Fund at Matrix Ltd. In his personal accounts, Mohr actively trades stocks, bonds, and mutual funds, but he does not invest in any fund that he manages. Matrix does not require any disclosures regarding personal trading, and Mohr makes no disclosures. Has Mohr violated Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts?
option_a: Yes.
option_b: No, since Matrix does not have any disclosure requirements.
option_c: No, since Mohr does not invest in any fund that he manages.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must deal fairly and objectively with all clients when providing investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment action, or engaging in other professional activities." Standard III(B) Fair Dealing requires Members and Candidates to treat all clients fairly when recommending investments or undertaking investment actions on their behalf. Members and Candidates must ensure their investment recommendations are disseminated in a way that provides all clients the fair opportunity to act on every recommendation. However, "fair" does not mean "equal." The Standard allows firms and analysts to offer higher levels of service to clients willing to pay a premium (Choice B). These services: must not disadvantage or negatively affect other clients and must be disclosed and available to all clients and prospective clients. In this scenario, Berger plans to offer the higher level of service (ie, follow-up calls) only to Brick Wall Bank's (BWB's) ten largest clients. Since she does not plan to offer this service to other clients, she violates the Standard. Although other clients do not currently do enough business with BWB to afford the service, they might wish to do more business with BWB or pay higher commissions if the additional service were offered to them (Choice A). Not disclosing the service to them gives them no choice.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
question_en: Zhao Fen, CFA, is an independent investor. She holds a large position of Formula Industries, a lightly traded stock with low liquidity, in one of her two personal accounts. If Zhao wishes to exit the position, which of the following would most likely violate the Standards?
option_a: Using an intermediary to sell the position outside of the market to avoid price impacts.
option_b: Selling her holdings as one position, which would likely cause a large drop in the price.
option_c: Trading the stock between personal accounts to attract interest from other market
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, or deceit or commit any act that reflects adversely on their professional reputation, integrity, or competence." Standard I(D) Misconduct is primarily concerned with the professional activities of a Member or Candidate, which covers all conduct that may negatively impact the Member's or Candidate's trustworthiness, reputation, or ability to perform their duties. Examples include acts that involve lying, cheating, theft, fraud, or other dishonest behavior. However, violations of Standard I(D) are not limited to actions specifically prohibited by the Standard. Failure to take appropriate action or lack of sufficient effort may also constitute a violation. However, there are other Standards that specifically address Emara's adding the broad-based equity fund (eg, V(A) – Diligence and Reasonable Basis; III(C) – Suitability). Standard I(D) addresses fraud and misconduct that erode public trust in the profession. Nothing in Emara's actions suggests that he committed fraud or deception, and asserting that Emara also violated Standard I(D) is an overbroad reading of the Standard (Choice C). (Choice B) Being arrested and jailed for acts of civil disobedience does not in itself constitute a violation of Standard I(D). In this case, Emara's protest activities are a form of civil disobedience that does not reflect poorly on his professional capacities.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
question_en: Ethan Clarke, CFA, is the Director of Research at Hogan Securities Ltd. Clarke hires an outside firm, Perkins Analytics Company (PAC), for external research. PAC maintains that the accuracy of its research is reliable since its source is publicly available data. Clarke believes this claim since PAC has an excellent reputation. Without further assessment, he communicates by email to all employees at Hogan Securities that the research is "good to use." Victoria Wheeler, CFA, makes recommendations to her clients based on PAC's investment research. In good faith, Wheeler relies on Clarke's approval that PAC's research is sound. Wheeler has no reason to question the process and procedures of third-party research since Clarke oversees Wheeler. With respect to Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis, the Standard was most likely violated by:
option_a: both Clarke and Wheeler.
option_b: Clarke only, by not performing due diligence on Perkins' research.
option_c: Wheeler only, by accepting Clarke's assessment of Perkins' research.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards." Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors requires Members and Candidates who supervise employees to encourage behavior that complies with local laws, rules established by their firms, and the Code and Standards. They also must take reasonable steps to detect and prevent violations. A Member or Candidate who encounters an inadequate compliance system should bring the shortcomings of the system to the attention of the company's managers and make recommendations for corrective actions. Any Member or Candidate who cannot perform supervisory responsibilities due to these shortcomings should decline to accept supervisory responsibility, in writing, until the compliance system is improved and allows for adequate controls. Accepting a supervisory role when the compliance system is inadequate would not allow the Member or Candidate to adequately monitor compliance by subordinates, and thus would violate the Standard. (Choice A) Smith has a duty to his employer to improve the compliance program using his best efforts but must decline the supervisory responsibilities of the job until the firm has committed to investing appropriate resources into the compliance program. (Choice C) The Standard does not require the Member or Candidate to resign but to decline the supervisory responsibilities of the job until the compliance program is sufficiently improved.

question_en: Karl Mahler, CFA, creates a mutual fund in Country A, where he is a resident. Mahler intends to sell the security in both Country A and Country B. The laws of Country A are more strict than the laws of Country B, and the laws of both countries are more strict than the Code and Standards. When selling the mutual fund in Country B, Mahler must adhere to the:
option_a: laws of Country A.
option_b: laws of Country B.
option_c: Code and Standards.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II Integrity of Capital Markets discusses the member's and candidate's responsibility to protect the integrity of the capital markets. Standard II(A) focuses specifically on the use of material nonpublic information. Trading with material nonpublic information ("insider trading") threatens market integrity, which relies on all market participants having fair access to information and no participant having the advantage of using information that is not widely available. The table below is a quick reference for determining whether Standard II(A) is violated: When a firm has material nonpublic information about a stock, it must try to ensure that trading does not violate the Standard. A ban on all trading in the stock is not always necessary or advisable. For example, if a firm acts as a market maker or dealer for a certain security, suspension of market making may signal that the firm has material nonpublic information and, in effect, expose that information. Market-making activities may continue but should be restricted to taking passive, counterparty positions in unsolicited trades. (Choice A) Risk-arbitrage activity (proprietary trading, as when a firm establishes positions for its own profit) should be suspended since there is great potential for illegal gains. (Choice C) The stock should be placed on a "restricted" or "watch" list, and employees should not trade the stock for their personal accounts. Personal trades should be reported periodically and monitored for insider trading activity.

question_en: Kathy Lee Wayne, CFA, is a portfolio manager who supervises a team at a large investment firm. Since the firm has adopted CFA Institute Code and Standards, Wayne assumes its compliance policies and procedures are adequate for monitoring her team. During her annual performance review, her supervisor tells Wayne that annual bonuses will be based only on hitting investment performance targets "no matter what it takes." Wayne replies, "That sounds fine. I'll let my team know, and my team will hit its targets!" Some months later, a member of Wayne's team admits to falsifying reports in order to make it appear that the team hit its performance targets. During the subsequent internal investigation, investigators conclude that Wayne did not participate in the falsification and could not be expected to have been aware of it. According to Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors, which of the following best describes how Wayne has not complied with recommended practice?
option_a: Only by failing to detect her employee's unethical activity
option_b: Only by readily accepting the incentive structure of the firm
option_c: Both by failing to detect her employee's unethical activity and by readily accepting the
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information requires Members and Candidates to abstain from investment actions if they have material nonpublic information (MNI). Trading on or acting on MNI erodes the public's trust in the fairness of the capital markets. MNI can come from many sources, and a Member or Candidate must evaluate information to decide whether it is MNI before acting on it. Selective disclosure (eg, analysts on a conference call, corporate insiders) does not necessarily make information public. In this question, Ching Liu and ES intentionally disclosed information and gave the analysts the timeline of when that information would be publicly disseminated. This type of selective disclosure is not a violation of the Standard (Choices A and B). However, by agreeing to be part of the select group receiving the information, Bo Wang has a duty to keep this information confidential until it is released publicly by the company. Even though Wang did not directly disclose the MNI, he violated the Standard by using his knowledge of MNI to influence others to act based on this information. Acting on MNI is not limited strictly to that company's securities (eg, ES), any trading based on MNI is a violation of the Standard.

question_en: Shani Gupta works in the manufacturing industry and wants to transition into a financial services role. She believes a CFA charter can help with this transition. Gupta recently sat for Level III of the CFA exam and is excited to update her resume to send to potential employers, although she has not yet received her results. Which of the following statements can she most appropriately use on her resume to adhere to the Standards?
option_a: "The knowledge gained from the CFA program makes me a superior candidate."
option_b: "I will be eligible for a CFA charter after completing my required work experience."
option_c: "My studies in the CFA program have enhanced my knowledge and skills in finance."
explanation_en: Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment. Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' interests before their employer's or their own interests." Under Standard VI(C), Members and Candidates must notify their employers, existing clients, and prospective clients of benefits or costs for client referrals. Disclosing referral arrangements allows employers and clients to determine if objectivity is compromised and to identify costs. Members and Candidates must properly disclose referral arrangements before clients sign up for a service that confers the benefits (eg, revenue, income). Before Long Ming signs new contracts, both Mao Yi and Jiang Bai, as parties to the arrangement, must disclose to Ming the details of the referral arrangement between them (Choice A). (Choice C) The Standard requires Members and Candidates, not their firms, to disclose referral fees to clients.

question_en: Andrei Ostrovsky, CFA has been employed as an advisor at Bolshoi Investments Inc. (BII) for several years. His employment agreement does not include a "noncompete" clause or termination policies. Ostrovsky decides to leave BII and start a new advisory firm. Prior to giving notice to his employer, Ostrovsky spends a few weekends setting up his new office. There he "connects" with as many of his clients as he can on social media, which is easy as he knows their names. Before leaving BII, he does not mention his departure from BII or his plans for his new firm to any client, on or off social media. One day after leaving BII, he posts a notice on a social media site that he has left BII and that he would be happy to continue to advise his former clients at his new firm. With regards to Standard IV(A) Loyalty, has Ostrovsky most likely violated the Standard?
option_a: No
option_b: Yes, by soliciting business from BII's clients
option_c: Yes, by "connecting" with BII's clients while still employed by BII
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards." Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors requires Members and Candidates who supervise other personnel to take reasonable steps to prevent and detect violations of laws and regulations. The Guidance to the Standard indicates that compliance with the Standard, at a minimum, requires supervisors to: establish written compliance procedures; and perform regular reviews to ensure that employees are following the procedures. A supervisor who does not satisfy these requirements violates the Standard even if no laws were broken. In this question, Grimaldi violated the Standard by not implementing a regular review to ensure that employees were complying with the requirement to provide confirmations for trades occurring in outside accounts. However, the concept of "reasonableness" does not make supervisors responsible for detecting all violations; employees may be able to evade compliance in ways that cannot be detected through reasonable efforts. It is not reasonable to conclude that Grimaldi knew or should have known in advance that an employee would try to evade the requirement by establishing a hidden account (Choices B and C). However, now that he knows it is possible, Grimaldi should update the fund's rules to prevent future occurrences.
